title: Generative AI-assisted feedback and EFL writing: a study on proficiency, revision frequency and writing quality
extended_summary:
This study examines whether AI-assisted writing feedback can improve EFL learners’ academic writing compared with traditional teacher feedback. The paper addresses a practical instructional question: whether a widely available AI writing assistant can support better writing outcomes, more revision activity, and stronger student engagement, while also probing concerns about overreliance and the limits of tool-generated feedback.

The intervention used Grammarly Premium as an AI-assisted feedback system. Sixty postgraduate EFL students in a mandatory English for Academic Purposes writing course were randomly assigned to an experimental group using Grammarly or a control group receiving traditional written teacher feedback. The intervention lasted 6 weeks within an 8-week course, and the same instructor taught both groups with standardized lesson plans. Students in the experimental group received a short training session on using Grammarly critically and were instructed to revise drafts using the tool’s feedback; the control group received delayed written feedback from the instructor.

The study found that the Grammarly group scored significantly higher on the post-test overall writing measure, with especially strong gains in language use and organization, but not in content. Within the experimental group, greater use of AI features and more revisions were positively associated with higher post-test performance. Interview data suggested that students perceived the tool as increasing efficiency, confidence, and grammar awareness, while also emphasizing the need for critical judgment and noting that the tool was weaker for broader language support such as fluency and style.

Overall, the paper concludes that AI-assisted feedback can improve certain dimensions of EFL writing when used thoughtfully, but it does not replace teacher support for higher-order writing concerns. The authors also caution that students should not rely passively on AI suggestions and that the tool’s benefits are concentrated in surface-level correction and revision support rather than content development.

identified_tools.name: Grammarly
identified_tools.description: An AI-powered writing assistant that provides automated feedback on grammar, spelling, punctuation, style, clarity, vocabulary, and limited rewrite suggestions, with plagiarism detection.
identified_tools.use_case: Used by the experimental group as Grammarly Premium for automated feedback and revision support on EFL writing tasks over a 6-week intervention, compared against traditional teacher feedback.

findings.finding_summary: In a quasi-experimental pre-test/post-test study with 60 postgraduate EFL students (n=30 Grammarly, n=30 control), the Grammarly group scored significantly higher on the total post-test writing score than the control group. Reported means were 54.37 (SD=5.54) vs 45.50 (SD=5.32), Welch's t(47.35)=10.89, p<0.001; Mann-Whitney U=16.50, z=6.42, p<0.001.
For the Content sub-score, the Grammarly group did not differ significantly from the control group. Means were 17.05 (SD=2.15) vs 16.10 (SD=2.30), t(58)=1.68, p=0.098.
findings.measure: Content sub-score of post-test writing rubric

findings.finding_summary: The Grammarly group outperformed the control group on Organization. Means were 18.12 (SD=1.95) vs 15.65 (SD=2.55), Welch's t(51.88)=4.31, p<0.001.
findings.measure: Organization sub-score of post-test writing rubric

findings.finding_summary: The Grammarly group outperformed the control group on Language Use. Means were 19.20 (SD=1.40) vs 13.75 (SD=2.80), Welch's t(40.15)=9.55, p<0.001, indicating a large advantage for the AI-assisted feedback condition on language/mechanics-related writing quality.
findings.measure: Language Use sub-score of post-test writing rubric

findings.finding_summary: Within the Grammarly group (n=30), higher frequency of using Grammarly features and higher revision counts were positively correlated with total post-test score. Significant correlations included generative AI feature use (practice r=0.346, assignment r=0.373), grammar/vocabulary feature use (practice r=0.374, assignment r=0.348), and total revisions (practice r=0.359, assignment r=0.375).
findings.measure: Correlations between feature use / revision frequency and total post-test score

findings.finding_summary: Within the Grammarly group (n=30), use of generative AI features was positively correlated with total revisions during both practice and assignment activities (practice r=0.421, assignment r=0.398), suggesting repeated use was associated with more revision activity.
findings.measure: Correlation between generative AI feature use and total revisions

findings.finding_summary: In hierarchical regression within the Grammarly group (n=30), assignment score explained 16.2% of variance in post-test scores, and adding generative AI usage increased explained variance by 11.3% (R2 from 0.162 to 0.275). Revision frequency did not significantly add explanatory power. The final model reported assignment score (β=0.38) and generative AI usage (β=0.34) as significant unique predictors.
findings.measure: Hierarchical multiple regression predicting post-test score

quality_tier_rationale: This is a single quasi-experimental mixed-methods study rather than a randomized field trial, and some outcomes rely on self-reported usage plus post-hoc correlations. The design is informative but has moderate risk of bias and limited generalizability.
impact_tier_rationale: The study reports large, statistically significant gains on total writing and especially language use, with the strongest effects well above the 0.20 threshold. Even the null content result is offset by substantial positive outcomes on the main writing measures.
